title: mesh-stl plugin: what it does and when to call it
when: an STL must be created or checked, or it is unclear how this plugin differs from mesh-build
statement: mesh-stl is a DSH bundle for geometry: it generates STL from verified families (fcc-cell, channel-spheres, double-layer-burner, packing, cad-porous), runs the stl_qa.py contract (watertight, winding, bodies, volume/area/bbox in mm), cleans up and writes a passport to stl/registry.csv. Three tools: stl_hints (these cards), stl_generate (the real generator with a preset, dry-run, params overrides), stl_check (QA + optional cleanup and passport).
recipe: start with stl_hints({query}) — rules with numbers from the experiments
stl_generate({family, preset, name}) → stl_generate({dryRun:true}) for a cheap plan check
stl_check({stl, cleanup:true, register:true}) — a PASS is mandatory before meshing

hand-off to mesh-build: mesh_build({route:'snappy', scaffold:true, caseDir:'<case directory>', stl:['<name>.clean.stl'], scaffoldOptions:{domainMin,domainMax,cellSize,locationInMesh}}) — a single STL without caseDir and domain options does not create a case
evidence: plugins/mesh-stl/index.js: stl_hints, stl_generate, stl_check; data/generators.json — families and presets; lib/skill.js — the agent instruction
verified by a live run: fcc_cell_d5_r049 → PASS, watertight, 11 348 triangles, 62.2183 mm³

title: Working without sim-project.json: STL in an empty directory
when: geometry/QA runs in a clean directory with no sim-project.json (or a minimal one)
statement: The mesh-stl tools work without a project profile: the report carries project:"defaults" and configured:false, relative paths are resolved from the current directory, the registry defaults to ./stl/registry.csv (the header is created automatically), and generator outputs go to ./stl/generated/<family>/. The “no project” gate is gone; if the registry is read-only the QA verdict is kept and the write is returned as registered:{ok:false,error,row}. Verified by an end-to-end run in /tmp: stl_generate(primitive) → stl_check(PASS, engine js) → mesh_build(snappy) → mesh_check(PASS) → mesh_deliver(DELIVERED).
recipe: stl_generate({family:'primitive', name:'cube', params:{size_mm:[10,10,10]}}) — the file appears in ./stl/generated/primitive/
need your own paths/thresholds — create sim-project.json (sim-core/schemas): units, caseRoots, gate.profiles, foam.installations
evidence: plugins/mesh-stl/index.js: withPortable() adds project/configured and a hint to next instead of a refusal
plugins/mesh-stl/lib/registry.js: registryFilePath() resolves from projectRoot, otherwise from cwd
run of 2026-11-26 in /tmp: 12 tri, PASS, 2584 cells, gate PASS, DELIVERED

title: Cone, pipe and parts[]: analytic volume checks the triangulation
when: a quick closed body is needed for a route or gate test, or a multi-body assembly must go into one STL without a CAD kernel
statement: The built-in `primitive` family emits box, sphere, cylinder, cone (apex or frustum), pipe (hollow cylinder with annular caps) and a `parts[]` assembly in plain JS — no python, no project data. Every body takes `center_mm`; each body or part accepts `translate_mm`, `rotate_deg` (degrees about the global X, then Y, then Z) and a uniform `scale`. `parts[]` writes ONE STL with several closed shells and `volume_mm3_theory` is the analytic sum, so `stl_check({expectVolume})` checks the triangulation instead of trusting it.
recipe: stl_generate({ family: 'primitive', params: { shape: 'pipe', radius_outer_mm: 3, radius_inner_mm: 2, height_mm: 10 } })
stl_generate({ family: 'primitive', params: { parts: [{ shape: 'box', size_mm: [10,10,10] }, { shape: 'cylinder', radius_mm: 2, height_mm: 10, translate_mm: [20,0,0] }] } })
stl_check({ stl, expectVolume: <analytic>, expectBodies: 1 }) — bodies = 1 + closed voids, so a parts[] assembly expects the shell count
evidence: plugins/mesh-stl/lib/shapes.js: coneTriangles, pipeTriangles (per-surface orientation), mergeTriangles, transformTriangles
experiments/_scratch/verify-a4.mjs: 15/15 — cone 94.096 vs pi*r^2*h/3 = 94.248, pipe 78.316 vs 78.540, parts 1125.31 vs 1125.66, rotated+scaled box 8000.0
pitfalls: a pipe is not convex: orienting the whole body outward would point the inner wall into the material, so each surface is oriented against an expected direction
rotate_deg is applied before translate and about the global axes in X→Y→Z order — not intrinsic rotations
a parts[] assembly is several shells in one STL: snappy meshes it, but `expectBodies` must be the shell count, not 1
